newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine peso may be edgy on oil deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso may be edgy on oil deregulation.

text.p: The Philippine peso could be volatile in coming months as dollar demand from oil companies increases due to the full deregulation of the domestic oil industry as of Saturday, analysts said.
But they said strong dollar inflows and a Central Bank armed with robust gross international reserves might smooth any turbulence in the foreign exchange market.
At the end of January, the Philippines' gross international reserves stood at $11.76 billion.

"There might be some pressure and the peso could possibly depreciate, but again you can't be certain. There could also be large (dollar) inflows," said Rafael Buenaventura, president of Philippine Commercial International Bank.
"I think what the Central Bank will do here is to try to smooth the volatility."
Full deregulation means that oil companies now have to face the risk of fluctuations in the peso-dollar exchange rate on the credit financing they obtain for their oil imports.
Previously, the government had taken on those risks by providing foreign exchange cover to oil firms.

Assistant Finance Secretary Gil Beltran told Reuters monthly dollar demand due to oil imports would double to $360 million in February and in March before easing back to the normal level of $180 million in April.
"The peso will depreciate by just a few centavos," said Beltran.
"The issue here is the timing of demand and supply," said Johnny Noe Ravalo, an economist with the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP).
The dollar could rise on some days at the Philippine Dealing System (PDS) when oil companies need to buy dollars from banks and inflows are light, he said.

The PDS is the computerised trading system for pesos and U.S. dollars used by member banks of the BAP. Dollar sales to oil companies are not done through the PDS but dollar demand is reflected in banks' bids for the U.S. currency.
However, "the foreign exchange market is deeper than it used to be years ago," Ravalo said, a factor which should lessen any volatility.
Total daily transactions at the PDS now average $200 million from last year's $110 million, the Central Bank has said.
Oil company officials said the peso was not likely to suffer from the deregulation of the oil industry because of the availability of dollar credit lines from banks.
"We don't see an immediate significant impact on foreign exchange," said Oscar Reyes, vice-president for finance at Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp.
"We can take the risk in foreign exchange loans because we don't believe the peso will depreciate that much," an official from another oil company said.
"There's a big advantage to borrow in dollars (when the peso is stable)," said ING Bank chief dealer Cesar Zulueta.
He noted that oil firms can borrow in dollars at a 6.5 percent interest rate while peso credit lines carry a 12 percent interest rate.
The peso had weakened slightly to 26.288 to the dollar at the close of 1996 from 26.228 at the start of the year. It finished at 26.348 on Friday, off its low of 26.35 this year.

But traders said oil companies would eventually have to buy dollars in exchange for pesos to settle their loans. The availability of dollar credit loans, however, gives banks the room to plan their purchases when the peso is strong, they said.
